To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the political arrangements of Pacific Asia, including the most democratic ones, are legitimised by non-liberal values.

(a) the adoption of democratic practices in Pacific Asia is primarily a strategy of the ruling state to manage the social and political consequences of rapid economic growth, and that (b) the adoption of democracy is not a sign of political liberalization, but rather a strategy of state-led political modernization.
(1) The political system of Pacific Asian countries has not been liberalized, but rather has been reorganized in the context of the economic transformation of these countries.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how and why the state is able to legitimate a particular form of democracy in the absence of a strong civil society.
the political implications of economic modernization and social transformation.
the question: how do Asian societies, in which the state plays a central role, deal with the challenges of modernization?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Asian experience with liberal democracy has been one of failure.
the political arrangements in Pacific Asia are illiberal, but democratic, and that this is the result of a state-led process of political change.
the Asian model of development is neither liberal nor democratic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the book is an exploration of how the political arrangements of the region are legitimised by non-egalitarian values and how the state has used democratic practices as a tool for political control.
it is a study of the political consequences of economic change.
it has shown that the political culture of Pacific Asia is neither the product of the past nor a response to the present but a combination of the two.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the political systems of Pacific Asia are best understood as illiberal democracies.
the political systems that have emerged in the region do not conform to the model of liberal democracy.
the political arrangements of contemporary Asia do not represent an aberration from the path of modernization, but a distinct and viable alternative.
